Training a tiny neural network: cat vs dog faces (AFHQ)

One weight per pixel — no hidden layer — see learning happen click by click

How to run this notebook Download this file, then in a terminal run: 

marimo edit --sandbox neural_network_training.py
If you do not have marimo installed, use pip install marimo or run without installing via uvx marimo edit --sandbox neural_network_training.py. The --sandbox flag creates an isolated environment and installs dependencies from the script header automatically. Local AFHQ images (required once): from the project root run uv run scripts/prepare_afhq_subset.py to download AFHQ via Hugging Face and write 220 small PNGs plus data/afhq_catdog/manifest.json. After that, the notebook only reads disk — no datasets package or large HF cache at class time.

What you'll learn in this module You will see how a linear classifier (a two-layer network with no hidden units) maps a tiny grayscale image to a single score, how that score picks cat vs dog, how the weight matrix lines up with the pixel grid, and how add / subtract updates change accuracy on held-out images.

What we want to do

We want a function that looks at an aligned cat or dog face and answers which it is. Data: faces are from AFHQ (prepared via Hugging Face huggan/AFHQ). A helper script resizes to a square grid (default ||(64\times64||)), converts to grayscale, and saves PNG files under data/afhq_catdog/ that this notebook loads directly — no dataset download when you open Marimo.

How we do it (architecture)

The PNG files are grayscale (luma ||(0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B||) was applied when building the bundle). One weight per pixel on that square grid (see grid_size in manifest.json). ||[ \text{output} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{H \times W} w_i x_i ||]Here ||(\mathbf{x}||) is the grayscale face grid flattened (pixels in about ||([0,1]||)). Decision rule: if ||(\text{output} > 0||) we predict dog; if ||(\text{output} \le 0||) we predict cat. Reshape ||(\mathbf{w}||) to an ||(H\times W||) matrix — same shape as the resized face — so every weight sits on top of the pixel it multiplies. Next to each training image you see that matrix update when you add or subtract the current image.

Train by clicking

Use Add (+) when the current training image should push the model toward dog: we add the pixel vector to ||(\mathbf{w}||). Use Subtract (−) when it should push toward cat: we subtract the pixel vector. Next only changes the training image. Randomize draws new random weights. After each add/subtract, we measure accuracy on a separate evaluation set and plot how it evolves versus the number of training clicks.
